title: Matot: children before sheep (Numbers 32:16, 24)
hookLine: two tribes mention sheepfolds first; Moses reverses it: build cities for your little ones
tomorrow: Matot: not while they fight alone

lines: A THREE-CAR GARAGE, AND THE SCHOOLS.
REUBEN AND GAD, AND THEIR HERDS.
A REQUEST, IN A PARTICULAR ORDER.
cards: Listen to how people describe a move. We found a place with a three-car garage, a big yard for the dog, and, oh, the schools are fine. Sometimes the order of a sentence tells you what someone's really thinking about.
The Torah listens to word order too. The tribes of Reuben and Gad have huge herds of cattle. They look at the land east of the Jordan, the land of Gilead, and see a place for cattle.
So they come to Moses with a request: let us settle here. And they put it in a particular order.

teach.b: Moses' first reaction is sharp, and that comes tomorrow. Then the two tribes come back with a plan.

In paraphrase: we'll build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones, and then we'll go and fight alongside everyone else until the land is won. Sheepfolds first. Then children.
Moses agrees to the plan. But when he repeats it back, he changes the order.
In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Build you cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep." Children first. Then sheep.
He doesn't lecture them. He just says it back the right way round.
Rashi, drawing on an older midrash, says this was exactly the point: they cared more for their property than for their sons and daughters, because they mentioned the cattle before the children.

teach.h: RASHI: MAKE THE MAIN THING MAIN.
teach.b: Moses told them, in effect, make the main thing the main thing. A tiny edit, two phrases swapped. The kind of edit a good friend makes when repeating your words back: you said the house and then the kids.
Did you mean it that way? Nobody's accusing the tribes of not loving their children. They were herders, and the cattle were their living.
Livestock are how you feed children. But the text notices how easily the means to an end slips into first place, and how a single sentence can reveal it. Moses' fix isn't a punishment.

teach.h: A PLAN THAT BEGINS WITH PEOPLE.
teach.b: It's a reordering, so that the plan begins with the people it's for.

how: The request of Reuben and Gad is read in the portion of Matot each summer, and Rashi's note on the order of sheepfolds and children is often taught alongside it.

the sheepfolds the two tribes built for their herds
the land east of the Jordan, good for grazing

games.q: who said it which way — tap the pairs.
p: green land east of the Jordan

s: Moses refused to let Reuben and Gad settle east of the Jordan
he agreed, on the condition that they fight alongside the others first.
Moses repeated their plan with the order reversed
build you cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep.
Rashi says the tribes didn't care about their children at all
he says they cared more for their property, because they mentioned it first.

games.q: you're Moses. two tribes propose a plan: sheepfolds for our cattle, and cities for our little ones. how do you answer?
o: accept it, but say it back with the children first.
games.why: he accepted the plan and said it back: build cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep.

practice: Say your week ahead back to yourself the way Moses did, the errands, the work, the purchases, the plans, and then ask: who is all this for?
Put their names first, and notice whether one thing on your list has quietly crowded out the people it was meant to serve.

wordCard.voice: Matot. The portion where two tribes mention sheepfolds before children, and Moses quietly turns the sentence around.

orig.note: Hebrew: cities for your little ones (Numbers 32:24); taf means little children.

carryVoice: Your line: children first. The order of a sentence can say a lot. See you tomorrow.
